title: The Lion-Makers

full_text:
In a flourishing university city in northern India lived four young Brahmins who had been companions since childhood. Three of them were scholars of prodigious intellect, having mastered the sacred scriptures, grammar, logic, and arcane esoteric sciences, but they were completely devoid of practical common sense. The fourth companion, named Subuddhi, or Good-Sense, had never studied ancient books, but possessed exceptional common sense and practical wisdom.

One day, the four youths resolved to travel to the courts of foreign kings to display their learning and win riches.

As they set out along the highway, the eldest scholar objected: 'Subuddhi has read no books; he has no scholarship! Why should we share the royal gifts with an uneducated companion? Let him return home!'

The second scholar agreed, but the third, who was generous, said: 'No, we have played together as brothers since our youth. Let him come; he shall receive his share of our earnings.'

As they walked through a dense forest, they came upon a clearing strewn with the dry, bleached bones of a dead beast.

The first scholar exclaimed: 'Here is an opportunity to demonstrate the miraculous power of our scientific learning! A creature lies dead before us; let us bring it back to life!'

The first scholar stepped forward: 'By the power of my knowledge of anatomy, I can assemble these scattered bones into their proper skeletal structure!' Chanting mantras, he assembled the skeleton: it was the complete skeleton of a colossal, ferocious lion!

The second scholar stepped forward: 'By my mastery of esoteric biology, I can clothe these bones with sinews, flesh, skin, and warm blood!' Chanting his spells, the bones were covered with muscular flesh, a bristling golden mane, and razor-sharp claws. The colossal beast lay upon the grass, complete in every feature, awaiting only the breath of life.

The third scholar stepped forward, raising his hands: 'Now, by the supreme science of vital animation, I will breathe the living soul into this frame!'

Seeing him prepare to animate the beast, the fourth companion, Subuddhi, seized his arm in alarm: 'Hold your hand, brother! Can you not see that this is a ferocious lion? If you bring this predator to life, he will instantly spring upon us and devour us all!'

The third scholar sneered with arrogant pride: 'Ignorant fool! Do you dare to forbid me from demonstrating the triumph of my scientific scholarship? I will not permit my learning to be wasted!'

Subuddhi replied calmly: 'If you are determined to create a monster, wait but a single minute until I have climbed into the high branches of yonder tree!'

Subuddhi scrambled up the trunk of a tall banyan tree, perching safely upon a stout bough.

The third scholar chanted his final, triumphant incantation. The breath of life entered the colossal beast: its golden eyes blazed; its nostrils flared, and with a thunderous roar that shook the forest, the famished lion sprang to its feet!

Seeing three fat, defenseless scholars standing before him, the ferocious beast leaped upon them with flashing claws, tearing all three learned men to pieces and devouring their flesh upon the spot.

Once the beast had eaten his fill and ambled away into the forest, Subuddhi climbed down from the tree in safety, returning home to his village, having learned that book-learning without common sense is fatal.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"Better is common sense by far than books and scholarly pride;
For learning without practical wit is ruin at your side;
Behold the three great scholars dead upon the forest floor,
Slain by the very lion's fangs their learning brought to roar."
moral: Mere book-learning and scholarship without practical common sense leads to swift and certain destruction.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The Lion-Makers"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
quiz.hint: Remember the moral lesson of this traditional story.

quiz.question: How do the characters overcome their challenge?
options: Through patience, calm reflection, and wisdom
By shouting loudly and blaming others
By running away from every problem
quiz.hint: Consider the virtues praised in world folklore.

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach young readers?
options: Honesty, kindness, and clear thinking lead to peace
quiz.hint: Reflect upon the resolution of the story.

author: Pandit Vishnu Sharma (~200 BCE – 300 CE)
content_notes: Family-safe traditional adaptation from the Panchatantra anthology.

vocabulary.meaning: wise advice given to guide decisions
the ability to judge well and understand the truth
the ability to remain calm and think clearly during sudden events

discussion_questions.prompt: What is the main situation at the beginning of "The Lion-Makers"?
Why does this story teach that "Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength."?
How could you use this lesson in your own school or family life?
Was the character’s final decision fair and kind to everyone?
Imagine an alternate peaceful ending or a new creative adventure for these characters.

reflection_prompt: Have you ever had to choose between acting quickly in anger or waiting patiently to understand the truth?
activity: Draw a colorful picture of your favorite moment in this story or share the moral with your family.
